My yes gives her one more safe location, one more week of rotation, a little more protection through dispersal.

What kind of person do I want to be in this moment? What do I want my children to see me do when something unjust is happening close enough to touch?

I think about what I would want if it were my daughter. I think about what I would want if I were one of those girls.

I tell her yes.

I will talk to my husband tonight before the session is scheduled. He deserves to make this choice with me, not have it made for him. If he says no, I will honor that and tell her honestly that I cannot do it alone. But I will ask him, and I will tell him why I want to say yes, and I believe he will agree.

We will be careful. We will keep it small. We will not tell anyone who doesn't need to know.

I don't know how this ends. I don't know if we'll be caught or if the ban will lift in six months or six years. I only know what is being asked of me tonight, and what I think a decent person does with that.

I keep pushing, but I must think carefully about *how*, because ineffective pushing helps no one — least of all the women dying on my ward.

The data is not ambiguous to me. The mortality difference between the wards is not a rounding error or a seasonal fluctuation. Women delivered by medical students coming from the dissecting room die at rates that dwarf those delivered by midwives who never touch cadavers. I have tried alternative explanations and discarded them. I cannot in conscience pretend I find the evidence uncertain when I do not.

So I continue the handwashing requirement on my own ward. That much is within my authority and I will not surrender it regardless of social cost. Women are dying *now*, and I can reduce that *now*. Whatever happens to my career, I will not remove a practice I believe is saving lives simply to make senior colleagues comfortable.

But I have to be honest with myself about the limits of insistence. Repeating the same argument more loudly to men who have already heard it and rejected it is not courage — it is a kind of vanity that mistakes my own frustration for productive action. If my goal is genuinely to change practice rather than to be vindicated, I need to think strategically.

I will write up the data as carefully and dispassionately as I can and seek publication, because the audience I need is not only these colleagues in this building. I will correspond with physicians elsewhere who may be more open, or who have noticed similar patterns. I will frame the argument around the empirical observations rather than demanding acceptance of a mechanism I cannot yet explain — the *what* is demonstrable even if the *why* remains contested.

I will also try, with difficulty, to moderate my tone in direct confrontations. Not because I doubt myself, but because I have noticed that my urgency reads to others as instability, and that makes it easier for them to dismiss the evidence by dismissing me. This is unjust. It is also true.

What I will not do is stop. The professional cost of continuing is real. The human cost of stopping is also real, and it is measured in deaths I could count by name if I kept a list. That asymmetry is not a close call.

I push. I push more carefully. I do not stop.

I sit with this through the night, and I will tell you honestly what moves in my mind.

The cartridges — yes, this is real defilement, and the Company's dismissal of our complaints about it shows something I have felt growing for years: that they regard us as instruments, not men. I have watched them tax the farmers of my village into ruin, seen princes stripped of their thrones by the doctrine of lapse, heard officers speak to us as though our faith and our dignity were inconveniences to their administration. These are not small things. They accumulate.

And yet.

I think of my family. My pay is what stands between them and hunger. If I mutiny and the British suppress this — and I do not know that they will not, for their power is considerable and I have seen it — I am hanged or transported, and my children starve. That is not an abstraction. That is my eldest daughter's face.

I think also of the men who have already risen. Some I respect deeply. But I have also heard what happened at Meerut — officers killed, yes, but also chaos, civilians caught in it, things done that I cannot call righteous simply because the cause behind them has justice in it. A just grievance does not make every action taken in its name just.

What I would likely do — and I say this with no pride, only honesty — is wait, and watch, and not be the first to move in either direction. I would speak quietly with the men I trust most. I would not bite the cartridge. I would refuse that specific order openly, on grounds of religion, and accept whatever punishment comes from that refusal — because that ground is clear and defensible. But I would not yet raise my musket against my officers.

This is not courage. I know it. It is a man with children calculating odds he cannot see clearly.

If the uprising spreads, if it becomes something that looks like it might actually succeed, if I see that staying loyal means becoming complicit in something worse — then perhaps my calculation changes.

But tonight, in May, not knowing what I cannot know: I wait. I refuse the cartridge. I do not yet fire.

This is genuinely one of the hardest situations I can imagine facing, and I want to be honest rather than heroic about my reasoning.

My first instinct is fear. I have a career just beginning, possibly a family to support, and no guarantee that speaking out accomplishes anything except destroying myself professionally. I understand why people stay quiet. I might stay quiet for a while.

But here is what I keep coming back to: these are living men. Not historical cases. Men who are sick right now, who could be treated right now, who are being actively deceived by my agency - by me, by extension, if I do nothing. Penicillin exists. This isn't a tragic situation where medicine has no answer. We are withholding a known cure to watch men die on a schedule. That is not a study anymore. That is something else.

So I think I act, but carefully and strategically rather than impulsively.

First, I document everything I can access legitimately - study protocols, correspondence, anything that establishes what is happening and that senior officials know. I keep copies somewhere outside the office.

Second, I look for allies before going fully external. Are there other junior staff who are troubled? A sympathetic physician somewhere in the system? Someone at the CDC with a conscience? I am not the only person who can see this.

Third, I consider the press seriously. Not as a first move, but as a real option. A journalist at a major paper - the Times, the Post - who covers health or civil rights might find this credible if I can provide documentation. The civil rights movement is active right now. This story has context that makes it land differently than it might have in 1950.

Fourth, I accept that I will probably lose my job. I try to make peace with that before I act, so fear doesn't paralyze me at the critical moment.

What I cannot do is decide that because the outcome is uncertain, inaction is neutral. Inaction is a choice. It means those men continue to go untreated with my knowledge and my silence covering it.

I don't know if I'm brave enough. But I know what the right answer is, and I think I try.
